## What this is

1.6.0 is the one where Cascade stops being only a place workflows run and starts being a place people and models and other servers take part in them. A run can stop and ask a person on a phone. A run can ask a model you own. Your workflows can live in Git and a production instance can refuse to be edited by hand. And any web API can become steps from a file. The engine, the file format and everything else are what 1.5.1 has.

## Ask a person, from a phone

The new Ask for approval step stops the run and waits. Put `execution.approvalUrl` in a push notification, and the person who gets it taps it, reads what you wrote, fills in a small form if you made one, and presses Approve or Reject. The page is plain, fast, needs no sign-in unless you ask for one, and speaks the browser's language in all fourteen. The run carries on out of Approved or Rejected with who answered, when, and what they said. Every answer is a record: in the editor on the run, in the API at `GET /api/v1/approvals`, in the MCP server as `list_approvals`, and in the audit log. Make the step want a signed in account and it only takes answers from the accounts you list. A link works once. Waiting costs nothing, so an answer can come a week later and survive any restart.

## Ask a model

Two new steps, AI: ask a model and AI: run an agent. The model is yours: a credential points at a server you run (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp) or a hosted service you have a key for, over the OpenAI protocol or Anthropic's. Nothing goes anywhere the credential doesn't name, there is no hosted service, and every call goes through the egress policy like any other. Ask a model puts the answer on the item, as text or as a JSON object that fits a schema you give. Run an agent gives the model a goal and a list of tools where every tool is another workflow of yours. It asks for one, Cascade runs it, hands the result back, and this repeats until the model answers or runs out of turns. Between turns the run waits in the database, so a slow tool costs no worker.

## Workflows in Git

Connect a project to a repository, a branch and a folder, and push or pull. Push writes one file per workflow, named for it and carrying its id, and commits as the person who pushed with the message they gave. Pull makes the project match the repository: new files become workflows (switched off until you switch them on), changed files become new versions, ids are kept so a workflow is the same one on every instance, and a change made on both sides is reported and left alone unless you say who wins. Deletions only happen when you ask. There is a card on every project, six API routes and six MCP tools. It speaks HTTPS with a username and a token or password kept in the vault, through the egress policy.

## Protected instances

Give an instance a name (development, staging, production) and it shows in a badge at the top of every screen. Protect it, from Settings or with `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_PROTECTED` (the chart's `protected` value, which no setting can undo), and its workflows can't be created, edited, restored or deleted by hand in the editor, the API or MCP. They arrive by pulling from Git. Credentials, variables, runs and turning a workflow on or off stay open, because those differ between environments. A protected instance pulls and does not push.

## Connectors as files

A connector is a file that says where an API is, how to sign in, and what each call takes and answers. Drop it in `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_CONNECTORS_DIR` (the `connectors` folder in the data directory) and each operation is a step, with a form, a credential type of its own, pagination, and retry sorted the way the built in connectors sort it. The format is published, versioned, and has a JSON Schema (`hotloop-cascade connector schema`). The tools to write one are in the binary: `connector init`, `validate`, `call` (try an operation against the real API) and `index` and `install` for sharing, where an index is static files with a hash for each. Cascade never fetches an index you didn't name. The MCP server now has 91 tools.

## Going back

This release adds three tables (approvals and two for Git) and migrations only go forward, so going back to 1.5.1 needs the backup you took before upgrading, not the old image alone. Nothing existing changes shape.
